board_events.text: Building a matrix from a recipe
A matrix is a filled-in grid: rows times columns, and every cell has an address.
The entry in row $i$, column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$.
$i$ = row, $j$ = column. Never swap them.
Given a rule $a_{ij} = f(i,j)$, walk the grid cell by cell and apply it.

board_events.text: Order $m \times n$ means exactly $m \times n$ cells — no more, no fewer.
A $2 \times 3$ matrix and a $3 \times 2$ matrix are different objects.
Counting without computing
Possible orders of an $N$-element matrix = number of divisors of $N$.
If $N$ is prime, only two orders exist: $1 \times N$ and $N \times 1$.
Number of distinct $m \times n$ matrices with entries from a $k$-set:
Each of the $mn$ cells is filled independently in $k$ ways.
Construction: substitute $i$ and $j$ into $a_{ij} = f(i,j)$.
Worked example: build a $2 \times 3$ matrix
Rule: $a_{ij} = 2i + 3j$, order $2 \times 3$ (so $i = 1,2$ and $j = 1,2,3$).
Fill row 1 fully, then row 2. Keep $i$ fixed, sweep $j$.
Worked example: a piecewise rule
Order $2 \times 2$, with $a_{ij} = i+j$ if $i \le j$, and $a_{ij} = i-j$ if $i > j$.
First decide which branch each cell uses by comparing $i$ and $j$.
Worked examples: counting orders and matrices
Ex 3: a matrix has 18 elements — how many possible orders?
Factor pairs: $1{\times}18,\ 2{\times}9,\ 3{\times}6,\ 6{\times}3,\ 9{\times}2,\ 18{\times}1$ — six orders.
If it had 7 elements (prime): only $1 \times 7$ and $7 \times 1$ — two orders.
Ex 4: how many $3 \times 3$ matrices with entries from $\{0,1\}$?

segments.text: <curious>What actually is a matrix? Strip away the fear and it is just a filled-in grid of numbers, arranged in rows and columns.
Every single cell in that grid has an address, and the whole game rests on respecting those addresses.
We write the entry sitting in row i and column j as a i j. So a two three lives in the second row, third column.
Lock this in: i always counts the row, j always counts the column. Swap them and every entry lands in the wrong cell.

Now, if someone hands you a recipe — a formula a i j equals f of i and j — you just walk the grid one cell at a time and apply that recipe. It is exactly like a cinema seating chart where the price depends on which row and which seat you are in.
Picture the grid: each box carries its own coordinates, its own address, and its own value.
The order, written m by n, tells you the grid has exactly m times n cells. Not one more, not one fewer — a matrix is never partially filled.
And order is an ordered pair: a two by three matrix is a genuinely different object from a three by two matrix, even though both hold six numbers.
Two little counting ideas hide in this topic, and both get examined every year. The beautiful part: neither needs any real computation — they are pure logic.

First: if a matrix has exactly N elements, how many possible orders can it have? Every way of writing N as rows times columns is one valid order. So the number of possible orders equals the number of divisors of N.
The fast route to that divisor count: factor N into primes, then multiply each exponent plus one together. That single product is d of N.
A neat special case: if N is a prime number, its only divisors are one and itself, so exactly two orders survive — one by N, and N by one.
Second idea: how many distinct matrices of a fixed order m by n can you build if every entry is chosen from a set of k allowed values?
The answer is k raised to the power m n.
Here is why: the grid has m times n cells, each one filled completely independently, and each has k choices — so you multiply k by itself m n times.
And to actually construct a matrix from a rule, you just substitute the row number i and column number j into the formula a i j equals f of i j, cell by cell.
Let us build one from scratch. This is the classic one-mark opener, and the only way to lose it is carelessness.
The rule is a i j equals two i plus three j, and the order is two by three. So i runs over one and two, j runs over one, two, three — six cells to fill.
Start with the top row, i equals one. a one one is two times one plus three times one, which is five. a one two is two plus six, that is eight.
a one three is two times one plus three times three — two plus nine — eleven.
Now drop to the second row, i equals two. a two one is four plus three, seven. a two two is four plus six, ten.
a two three is four plus nine, thirteen.
Assemble them in place and the matrix is five, eight, eleven on top; seven, ten, thirteen below.
The discipline that keeps you error free: fix the row, sweep across the columns, then move to the next row. Never jump around.
Same skill, one twist: the rule now branches. The recipe changes depending on how i compares to j, so the very first move in each cell is a comparison, not a calculation.
The definition: a i j equals i plus j when i is less than or equal to j, but i minus j when i is strictly greater than j. Two by two, so four cells.
For every cell, decide the branch before you compute. Ask: is the row index at most the column index, or bigger?
a one one: i equals j, one and one, so that satisfies i less than or equal to j. Use i plus j — one plus one is two.
a one two: i is one, j is two, so i is less than j. Again the i plus j branch — one plus two is three.
a two one: now i is two, j is one, so i is strictly greater than j. Switch to i minus j — two minus one is one.
a two two: i equals j again, so i plus j — two plus two is four.
The matrix is two, three on top; one, four below. Notice the trap the examiner is hoping for: rushing into arithmetic and forgetting to check the condition first.
Two counting problems back to back — this is where the divisor idea and the k to the m n idea earn their marks.
Example three: a matrix has eighteen elements. How many possible orders? We just count the ways to write eighteen as rows times columns.
Fastest path: factor eighteen as two times three squared. The divisor count is one plus one, times two plus one — that is two times three — six.
And you can list them to be sure: one by eighteen, two by nine, three by six, six by three, nine by two, eighteen by one. Six orders, exactly matching the divisor count.
The follow up: what if it had seven elements? Seven is prime, so its only divisors are one and seven — just two orders, seven by one and one by seven.
Example four flips to the other principle. How many distinct three by three matrices can you build using only the entries zero and one?
Nine cells, each filled two ways: two to the ninth power, which is five hundred twelve.

<excited>And a two by two matrix over the set one, two, three? Four cells, three choices each: three to the fourth — eighty one. Same principle every time: choices per cell, raised to the number of cells.

sections.title: Traps in construction and counting & related topics

board_events.text: Traps in construction and counting
Swapping $i$ and $j$ while building — the number-one error.
$m \times n$ and $n \times m$ are different orders — do not merge them.
For 'possible orders', count divisors — do not drop a factor pair.
In $k^{mn}$: base = choices per cell, exponent = number of cells. Do not flip them.
Pro-tip (orders): prime-factor $N$, multiply the (exponent$+1$)s.
Pro-tip (matrices): (choices per cell) raised to (number of cells), always.
Memory aid: 'i before j — row before column.'
Position carries meaning
Rows = trains, columns = classes, each cell = one fare. That grid of numbers is a matrix.
Entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $a_{ij}$; the whole matrix $A = [a_{ij}]_{m \times n}$.
$a_{23} \ne a_{32}$ in general — position is not interchangeable.

segments.text: <whisper>Here is where the easy marks quietly leak away. Four traps, and every one is avoidable.
Trap one, the big one: swapping i and j while constructing. If you let j drive the row, every entry lands in the wrong place and the whole matrix is wrong.
Trap two: treating m by n and n by m as the same order. They are not. A two by three and a three by two are different matrices, full stop.
Trap three, on the orders question: miscounting divisors — usually by forgetting that each factor pair counts twice, once each way, unless the number is a perfect square.
Trap four, on the counting question: flipping the base and exponent. The base is how many choices each cell has; the exponent is how many cells there are. Never the reverse.
Two pro-tips to bank. For possible orders: prime-factor N, then multiply each exponent plus one. Done in seconds.
For number of matrices: it is always choices per cell raised to the number of cells. One formula, no exceptions.
And the anchor that fixes the whole topic: i before j — row before column.

Picture the reservation board at New Delhi station. Trains run down the left — Rajdhani, Shatabdi, Duronto. Travel classes run across the top — first A C, second A C, third A C, sleeper. Every cell holds one fare.
Strip that board down to just the numbers and you have a matrix — a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns.
We name the entry in row i, column j as a i j, and the whole matrix as A equals the array a i j, of order m by n, where m is the number of rows and n the number of columns.

Here is the idea everything hangs on: position carries meaning. The number in row two, column three is not the same as the one in row three, column two — one might be the second A C Shatabdi fare, the other the sleeper Duronto fare.
On the board you can see it: a three by four grid, rows first, columns second, with the cell at row two, column three singled out as a two three.

Now the operations. Suppose the railways add a festival surcharge board with the same layout. To get the new fares, you add the two boards cell by cell — that is matrix addition, and it only works because the layouts match.
If instead every fare rises ten percent, you multiply every single cell by one point one. One ordinary number stretching the whole grid — that is scalar multiplication.

The third operation, matrix multiplication, is the tricky one, because it is not done cell by cell. Picture a sweet-shop bill: a row of quantities meets a column of prices to produce a total. That row-meets-column handshake is the whole idea.
And two hidden conditions bite immediately: addition and subtraction demand identical orders, while multiplication demands that the columns of the first match the rows of the second.
Before the operations, meet the family — the special shapes that keep reappearing in exam questions.

A row matrix is a single row, order one by n. A column matrix is a single column, m by one. A square matrix has equal rows and columns, n by n — and squareness is what unlocks inverses and powers later.
A diagonal matrix is square with every off-diagonal entry zero. A scalar matrix goes further: it is diagonal with all the diagonal entries equal to each other.
Push that once more and you get the identity, written I n — a scalar matrix with every diagonal entry equal to one. Its opposite in spirit is the null or zero matrix, every entry zero.
A triangular matrix is either upper, with zeros below the diagonal, or lower, with zeros above it.
One number attached to any square matrix is its trace — the sum of the diagonal entries, a one one plus a two two, and so on down the diagonal.
Now equality. Two matrices are equal only if two things hold: they share the same order, and every corresponding entry matches — a i j equals b i j for all i and j.

That definition is quietly powerful. A single two by two matrix equation is secretly four ordinary scalar equations bundled together — which is exactly how the board's favourite find-the-unknowns problems get solved.
<curious>Matrices behave like numbers just often enough to lull you — and then they spring three shocks that ordinary algebra never prepared you for.

First, why is multiplication a row-times-column sum rather than cell by cell? Because it encodes chaining two processes: first apply B, then apply A. The entry in row i, column j must gather every path from input j to output i, and that is a sum over the shared middle index.
That is the rule: the i j entry of A B is the sum over r of a i r times b r j. The shared index r is exactly why the inner dimensions must agree.
Shock one: multiplication is non-commutative. In general A B is not equal to B A, even when both products exist.

Take A as one, one, zero, one and B as one, zero, one, one. Then A B comes out two, one, one, one, but B A comes out one, one, one, two. Genuinely different matrices — the order of multiplication matters.
Shock two, and this one really stings: A B equal to the zero matrix does not force either A or B to be zero.

Watch: the matrix that keeps only the first coordinate, times the matrix that keeps only the second, gives the zero matrix — yet neither factor is zero. The familiar rule, if a product is zero a factor is zero, is simply false for matrices.
Shock three follows from it: cancellation fails. A B equal to A C does not let you conclude B equals C. You can never just cancel a matrix out of an equation.
Here is the formal rulebook — the three operations, with the exact condition each one demands.
Addition is entrywise: the i j entry of A plus B is simply a i j plus b i j. The non-negotiable condition is identical order — the same m by n on both.
Scalar multiplication is even simpler: the i j entry of k A is k times a i j. This one has no order restriction — you can scale any matrix.
Multiplication is the deep one: the i j entry of A B is the sum over r of a i r times b r j. If A is m by n and B is n by p, the product A B is m by p.

The gatekeeper is conformability: the columns of the first must equal the rows of the second. Say it as inner match, outer survive — the inner numbers must agree, and the outer pair becomes the result's order.
Addition's properties feel familiar: it is commutative and associative, the zero matrix is the additive identity, and minus A is the additive inverse — all of these requiring equal orders.
Scalar multiplication distributes cleanly: k times A plus B equals k A plus k B; k plus l, times A, equals k A plus l A; and k l times A equals k times l A.

Multiplication is associative and distributive, and the identity leaves a matrix unchanged: I m times A equals A equals A times I n. But remember — it is not commutative, and A B equal to the zero matrix does not make a factor zero.

sections.title: Solve a matrix equation for four unknowns & related topics

board_events.text: Worked example: solve for four unknowns
Step 1: carry out the scalar multiplications and the addition on the left.
Equality → equate corresponding entries → four scalar equations.
Worked example: which products even exist?
$A$ is $3\times 2$, $B$ is $2\times 4$, $C$ is $4\times 3$. Which of $AB, BA, BC, (AB)C, A(BC)$ are defined?
Do not compute entries — just chain orders and check inner matches.
$(AB)C$ and $A(BC)$ agree — a quiet confirmation of associativity.
Worked example: a power that reveals a pattern
The top-right entry counts up by one each time — conjecture the pattern.
Verify by induction: $A^{k}A = A^{k+1}$ keeps the form, top-right $k \to k+1$.

$AB$ is NOT $[a_{ij}b_{ij}]$ — it is the row-times-column sum.

segments.text: This is the board's bread and butter: a single matrix equation hiding four unknowns.
We are given two times the matrix a, b, c, d, plus three times the matrix one, minus one, zero, two, all equal to five, one, six, sixteen.
Step one: do the arithmetic on the left. Multiply the first matrix by two, the second by three, and add them together.
The left side collapses to a single matrix: two a plus three, and two b minus three on top; two c, and two d plus six below.
Now the key move: two matrices are equal only when corresponding entries match. So this one matrix equation splits into four separate scalar equations.
Top row: two a plus three equals five gives a equals one. Two b minus three equals one gives b equals two.
Bottom row: two c equals six gives c equals three. Two d plus six equals sixteen gives d equals five.
So a is one, b is two, c is three, d is five. The whole method is just this: simplify the left, then read off four little equations.
This is a speed trap. The slow student starts computing entries; the fast student never multiplies a single number.
We have A of order three by two, B of order two by four, and C of order four by three. The question asks which of five products are defined, and their orders.
The trick: write the orders side by side and check only the inner numbers. If they match, the product exists and inherits the outer pair.
A B is three by two, times two by four. Inner numbers are two and two — they match — so A B exists and is three by four.
B A is two by four, times three by two. Inner numbers are four and three — they clash — so B A is simply not defined.
B C is two by four, times four by three. Inner four and four match, so B C exists and is two by three.
For the chained ones: A B, times C, is three by four times four by three, giving three by three. And A, times B C, is three by two times two by three, also three by three.

Powers of a matrix look terrifying, but a good one hides a pattern you can spot from the first two steps.
We are told A is one, one, zero, one, and some power A to the n equals one, two thousand twenty six, zero, one. Find n.
Build from the bottom. A squared is A times A. Multiply it out and the top-right entry becomes two — you get one, two, zero, one.
A cubed is A squared times A, and now the top-right is three — one, three, zero, one.
The pattern is loud: the diagonal stays one, the bottom-left stays zero, and the top-right simply counts up by one at each power.
So we conjecture A to the n is one, n, zero, one.
Make it rigorous with induction: assume A to the k is one, k, zero, one; multiply by A and the top-right ticks from k to k plus one, completing the step.
Now just match the given matrix: the top-right is two thousand twenty six, so n equals two thousand twenty six.
<excited>Here is an Advanced-level problem that looks impossible — a sum of two thousand twenty five matrix powers — until one observation collapses the whole thing.
We have A equals two, minus one, three, minus two, and we want S, the sum of A plus A squared plus A cubed, all the way to A to the two thousand twenty five.
Never brute-force it. Probe the structure first: square A. Work through the entries and, remarkably, A squared comes out as the identity matrix.
That single fact — A squared equals I — collapses every power into just two values: every even power is the identity, and every odd power is A itself.
So the sum only needs a head count. Among the exponents one through two thousand twenty five, there are one thousand thirteen odd ones and one thousand twelve even ones.
Therefore S is one thousand thirteen copies of A, plus one thousand twelve copies of the identity.
Write that out: one thousand thirteen times the matrix two, minus one, three, minus two, plus one thousand twelve times the identity.

Add entrywise and S comes out three thousand thirty eight, minus one thousand thirteen, three thousand thirty nine, minus one thousand fourteen. The entire problem turned on spotting A squared equals I early.

Done honestly, A plus B all squared is A squared plus A B plus B A plus B squared — with A B and B A kept separate, not collapsed into two A B.
Trap three: believing that if A B is the zero matrix, some factor must be zero. Two non-zero matrices multiplying to zero is completely routine, so you can never cancel a matrix out of an equation.
Trap four: checking the wrong dimensions for conformability. Look at the inner numbers, not the outer ones — inner match, outer survive.

board_events.text: A 'who owes whom' ledger flips sign across the diagonal: $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$.
That forces the diagonal to zero: 'how much you owe yourself' is 0.
The transpose $A^{T}$ turns rows into columns — reflection across the diagonal.
Every square matrix splits: $\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{T})$ symmetric $+\ \frac{1}{2}(A-A^{T})$ skew.
The property toolkit
For any square $A$: $A+A^{T}$ is symmetric and $A-A^{T}$ is skew-symmetric.
For any matrix $A$ (any order): $AA^{T}$ and $A^{T}A$ are symmetric and square.

Picture a distance chart on the back of a road atlas — cities down the side, the same cities across the top. Delhi to Jaipur reads exactly the same as Jaipur to Delhi. The entry at row i, column j equals the entry at row j, column i.
A square matrix with that perfect balance is called symmetric: it is identical to its own reflection across the main diagonal.
You can see it on the board — fold the grid along the diagonal and the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Now flip to a who-owes-whom ledger among friends. If Ravi owes Sita five hundred, then from Sita's side it reads minus five hundred. The entry at i, j is the exact negative of the entry at j, i.
And what sits on the diagonal? How much you owe yourself — necessarily zero. So a skew-symmetric matrix is forced to have every diagonal entry zero.
The tool that makes both ideas precise is the transpose, written A with a capital T. It simply turns rows into columns — exactly that reflection across the diagonal.
With it the definitions become crisp: A is symmetric when A transpose equals A; A is skew-symmetric when A transpose equals minus A.

And here is the payoff the exam loves: every square matrix is secretly a blend of the two. Half of A plus A transpose is a symmetric part; half of A minus A transpose is a skew part; and they add back to A exactly.
Before any worked example, stock the toolkit — a handful of facts that turn most questions into one-line answers.

Fact two, true even for non-square A: both A times A transpose, and A transpose times A, come out symmetric — and square, whatever the shape of A.
Powers behave well too. Every power of a symmetric matrix is again symmetric.
For a skew-symmetric matrix the parity matters: even powers turn symmetric, odd powers stay skew. So the square of a skew matrix is symmetric, its cube is skew, and so on.
For two symmetric matrices A and B: A B plus B A is symmetric, A B minus B A is skew, and the product A B itself is symmetric only when A and B commute — that is, only when A B equals B A.
For two skew-symmetric matrices: A plus or minus B is skew, A B minus B A is skew, but A B plus B A flips to symmetric.
One striking fact: the only matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric at once is the null matrix, since A transpose equal to both A and minus A forces A to be zero.

The diagonal entry becomes a i i equals minus a i i. Move it across: two a i i equals zero, so a i i equals zero. Every diagonal entry must vanish.
Careful with the converse — it fails. A matrix can have a zero diagonal without being skew-symmetric; the off-diagonal sign-flip condition still has to hold.

Symmetric part $P = \tfrac12(A+A^{T})$.

Picture a UPI transaction. A refund of the exact amount reverses a payment perfectly — that is the inverse. segments.text: Now a question that tests whether a matrix can be inverted at all. A is one, minus three; minus two, six.
The full-proof way is to start reducing. Write A beside the identity.
There is the augmented block, ready to reduce.
Clear the minus two below the leading one: row two becomes row two plus twice row one. The left half of row two collapses to zero, zero.
That is the signal. A full row of zeros has appeared in the left block, so it can never become the identity — A is not invertible. Stop reducing.
The speed way spots it in one glance: the second row, minus two and six, is exactly minus two times the first row, one and minus three.
Whenever one row is a scalar multiple of another — or more generally a combination of the others — the matrix is singular and has no inverse.
So A inverse simply does not exist. Recognizing proportional rows up front saves the whole reduction.
Step up to a three by three — an upper-triangular one, which is the friendly case — and then a property saves us a second computation.
A has ones on the diagonal, two and three in the top row, a four in the middle row, and zeros below the diagonal.
Write A beside the identity and clear the entries above the diagonal, working from the bottom row upward so you never undo your own progress.
First, using the bottom pivot: row two becomes row two minus four times row three, and row one becomes row one minus three times row three.
Then, using the middle pivot: row one becomes row one minus two times row two. The left block is now the identity.
So the inverse is one, minus two, five; zero, one, minus four; zero, zero, one — still upper-triangular, as expected.
Now the second ask: the inverse of A transpose. Do not reduce again — use the property that the inverse of the transpose equals the transpose of the inverse.
So just transpose the answer you already have: one, zero, zero; minus two, one, zero; five, minus four, one.
One identity turned a second full row-reduction into a free transpose — that is the payoff of knowing the structural properties.

<excited>Here is the slickest way to invert a matrix — when it hands you a polynomial equation it satisfies. We are told A cubed minus three A plus two I equals the zero matrix, and asked to show A is invertible and find its inverse.

board_events.text: Four self-referential square matrices
Idempotent: $A^{2}=A$ — applying it twice changes nothing, so $A^{n}=A$.
Involutory: $A^{2}=I$ — its own inverse, $A^{-1}=A$ (a mirror flip).
Nilpotent: $A^{k}=O$ for some $k$; the smallest such $k$ is the index.
Idempotent: $I-A$ is also idempotent; the only invertible idempotent is $I$.
Involutory: even powers give $I$, odd powers give $A$.
Nilpotent matrices are never invertible.
Orthogonal: rows (and columns) are mutually perpendicular unit vectors — rotations.
The trace of a square matrix
Surprising: $AB\ne BA$ in general, yet their traces always agree.
So $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$ always — a favourite JEE one-liner.
Trace is linear: it distributes over sums and pulls out scalars.
Evaluating a polynomial at a matrix
Replace $x$ by $A$ and the constant $c$ by $cI$ — that is $f(A)$.
A square matrix very often satisfies an equation $f(A)=O$ of its own.
That single fact unlocks high powers AND the inverse — cheaply.
For the inverse: rearrange to $A\,(\text{poly})=cI$, then divide by $c$.
For high powers: use the relation to reduce $A^{2}$ (or higher) to lower terms.
Special types, trace, polynomials — the rulebook
Idempotent: $A^{n}=A$. Involutory: even $\to I$, odd $\to A$.

segments.text: <curious>Beyond the core operations, a handful of square matrices have a self-referential personality — square them, or multiply by their own transpose, and something remarkably simple comes back. Four types matter for JEE.

First, idempotent: A squared equals A. Such a matrix is absorbed by repetition — apply it once and applying it again changes nothing, so every power A to the n is just A again. Think of a projection: casting a shadow twice gives the same shadow.
Second, involutory: A squared equals I. The matrix is its own inverse, so A inverse equals A. Applying it twice undoes it — like a mirror flip.
Third, nilpotent: some power A to the k equals the zero matrix. The smallest such k is called the index. A nilpotent matrix eventually annihilates everything.
Fourth, orthogonal: A times A transpose, and A transpose times A, both equal the identity — which means the inverse is simply the transpose, A inverse equals A transpose.
Each carries a consequence. For an idempotent A, the matrix I minus A is also idempotent, and the only invertible idempotent matrix is the identity itself.
For an involutory matrix, powers alternate cleanly: even powers give the identity, odd powers give A.
A nilpotent matrix can never be invertible — a matrix that eventually sends everything to zero has no undo.
And an orthogonal matrix has rows, and columns, that are mutually perpendicular unit vectors; rotations are the classic example, and its inverse is free to write down.
One number captures a lot about a square matrix: its trace.
The trace is simply the sum of the diagonal entries — a one one plus a two two, all the way down.
It behaves linearly. The trace of a sum is the sum of the traces.
A scalar pulls straight out — trace of k A is k times trace of A — and transposing changes nothing, since the diagonal is untouched: trace of A transpose equals trace of A.
And the surprising identity: the trace of A B equals the trace of B A.
That one is a genuine shock, because A B and B A are usually different matrices — yet their diagonals always sum to the same number.
A direct consequence the examiners love: the trace of A B minus B A is always zero. It is a favourite one-line trap.
So hold the trace as a linear gadget: it distributes over sums, pulls out scalars, ignores transposes, and cannot tell A B from B A.
Here is one of the most powerful ideas in the chapter: you can feed a matrix into a polynomial.
Just replace the variable x by the matrix A, and replace the constant term c by c times the identity. That gives f of A.
For example, if f of x is x squared minus two x minus three, then f of A is A squared minus two A minus three I — the plain three becomes three times the identity.
The remarkable thing is that a square matrix very often satisfies a polynomial equation of its own — some f of A equals the zero matrix.
And that single relation is a master key: it unlocks both high powers of A and the inverse of A, with almost no computation.
For the inverse, rearrange the relation into A times some polynomial equals c times the identity, then divide by that non-zero c — exactly the trick from the last subtopic.
For high powers, use the relation to rewrite A squared, or higher, in terms of lower powers, and cascade downward.
For instance, if A squared equals two A plus three I, then A cubed is A times A squared, which becomes two A squared plus three A — and you keep collapsing, no brute force needed.
The consolidated rulebook for this subtopic — the definitions and identities you actually reach for.

Nilpotent means some power A to the k is the zero matrix — and such a matrix is never invertible; orthogonal means A times A transpose is the identity, so the inverse is just the transpose.
The trace: the sum of diagonal entries, linear over sums, and it pulls scalars out.
Two more trace facts: it is unchanged by transposing, and the trace of A B equals the trace of B A even when the products differ.
Evaluating a polynomial at a matrix: replace the variable by A, and every constant by that constant times the identity.
And the inverse trick in one line: if f of A is the zero matrix, rearrange to A times a polynomial equals c times I, then A inverse is one over c times that polynomial.
Two power shortcuts to bank: for an idempotent matrix every power is just A; for an involutory matrix, even powers give the identity and odd powers give A.

board_events.text: Worked example: verify $f(A)=O$, then invert
Now exploit it: from $A^{2}-2A-3I=O$, isolate a factor of $A$.
One identity gives both the verification AND the inverse — no row reduction.
Worked example: simplify using $A^{2}=A$
Idempotence collapses every power of $A$ back to $A$; $I$ commutes with all.
The $-7A$ term is engineered to cancel the collapse exactly.
Answer: $I$. No entries, no order given — pure structure.
Worked example: a real sales model
(i) Total units per product = add the two month-rows.
So 75 pens, 55 notebooks, 50 erasers.
(ii) Revenue per month = $Mp$ (units times prices).
Addition gives 'totals'; multiplication gives 'units $\times$ price' — the operations are the model.
Pro-tips for special matrices
Trace trap: $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ even though $AB\ne BA$.
Idempotent collapse: every power is $A$, so $A^{n}=A$ — never expand.
Involutory: even powers $\to I$, odd $\to A$; this crushes long power sums.
Nilpotent is always singular; orthogonal gives $A^{-1}=A^{T}$ for free.
Matrix-polynomial: from $f(A)=O$ with non-zero constant, factor out $A$ for $A^{-1}$.

segments.text: Now we put matrix polynomials to work, on a problem that first verifies an identity and then uses it to invert.
The matrix is A equals one, two, two, one, and we must show A squared minus two A minus three I is the zero matrix, then find A inverse.
Square A first. Multiply it by itself: A squared comes out five, four, four, five.
Write the other pieces: two A is two, four, four, two; and three I is three, zero, zero, three.
Now combine entrywise: five minus two minus three is zero on the diagonal, and four minus four is zero off it — the whole thing is the zero matrix. The identity is verified.
Now exploit that relation to invert. Start from A squared minus two A minus three I equals zero, and isolate a factor of A.

Move the three I across: A squared minus two A equals three I. Factor A on the left: A times the quantity A minus two I equals three I. Divide by three: A times one-third of A minus two I equals the identity.
So A inverse is one-third of A minus two I, which works out to minus one-third, two-thirds, two-thirds, minus one-third.
One identity delivered both the verification and the inverse — not a single row operation needed.
This one shows how a defining property turns a scary expansion into a one-liner. A is idempotent, and we simplify the cube of I plus A, minus seven A.
The setup: A squared equals A. That is the only fact we use.
The key: idempotence collapses every power of A back to A, and the identity commutes with everything, so the binomial expansion behaves exactly like ordinary algebra here.
Expand the cube of I plus A: it is I plus three A plus three A squared plus A cubed.
Now collapse the powers. A squared is A, and A cubed is also A, so three A squared plus A cubed becomes three A plus A, four A in total — the whole cube is I plus seven A.
Subtract the seven A: I plus seven A minus seven A leaves exactly the identity.
Notice the problem was engineered — the minus seven A term is precisely what cancels the collapsed expansion.
The answer is simply I, reached with no entries and no order given at all — pure structure.
To close the subtopic, a genuinely applied problem — the kind CBSE asks for four to six marks — showing that the operations are not decorative, they are the model.

A stationery seller records two months of unit sales of three products — pens, notebooks, erasers — as a matrix M, with months as rows and products as columns. The selling prices form a column vector p: fifty, twenty, ten rupees.
Part one asks for the total units sold of each product. Since the two rows are the two months, you just add them.
Add row one and row two entrywise: forty plus thirty-five, twenty-five plus thirty, thirty plus twenty — seventy-five, fifty-five, fifty.
So across both months: seventy-five pens, fifty-five notebooks, fifty erasers.
Part two asks for each month's revenue — that is units times prices, which is the matrix product M times p.
Multiply: month one is forty times fifty, plus twenty-five times twenty, plus thirty times ten — two thousand eight hundred. Month two works out to two thousand five hundred fifty.
So month one earns two thousand eight hundred rupees, month two two thousand five hundred fifty, for a grand total of five thousand three hundred fifty.
Notice the division of labour: addition handled the totals, and multiplication handled units times price. The matrix operations are literally the business model.
A cluster of pro-tips that turn these special matrices into fast marks.
The trace trap: remember that the trace of A B equals the trace of B A, even though A B and B A are usually different matrices. Examiners set this precisely to catch the unwary.
Idempotent collapse: if A squared equals A, then every power of A is just A. Never expand — collapse.
Involutory shortcut: even powers give the identity, odd powers give A. This crushes a long sum of powers into a simple head count of odds and evens.
Two more: a nilpotent matrix is always singular, so it has no inverse; and an orthogonal matrix hands you its inverse for free, since A inverse equals A transpose.
The matrix-polynomial move once more: whenever f of A is the zero matrix and the constant term is non-zero, factor out A and read off the inverse directly.
In application problems, map the operation to the meaning: addition combines or totals, and multiplication pairs units with a rate or price.
<whisper>The meta-tip across all of these: read the defining property first. Nine times out of ten it replaces the arithmetic entirely.

$AB\ne BA$; $\ IA=AI=A$; $\ AB=O$ need not give $A=O$ or $B=O$.
Deferred to Ch. 4: the test $|A|\ne0$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{|A|}\,\mathrm{adj}\,A$.
Rapid-recall cheat sheet
Construct: row $i$ then column $j$; orders = divisors of $N$; matrices = $k^{mn}$.
Multiply: 'inner match, outer survive'; $AB\ne BA$; never cancel a matrix.
'Transpose a product, turn it around': $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$.
'Symmetric adds, skew subtracts' (both over 2); skew's diagonal is asleep.
Special: idempotent $A^{2}=A$, involutory $A^{2}=I$, nilpotent $A^{k}=O$, orthogonal $A^{-1}=A^{T}$.
Inverse: $[A\mid I]\to[I\mid A^{-1}]$; 'zero row, no go'; $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
Matrix-polynomial: from $A\,(\text{poly})=cI$, divide by $c$ for $A^{-1}$.
Anchors: 'row before column'; 'inner match, outer survive'; 'zero row, no inverse'.
Coming in Ch. 4: the $|A|\ne0$ test and the adjoint inverse.

segments.text: <whisper>Here is your complete Matrices toolkit — one board that consolidates the whole chapter. Nothing new; just everything in one place for the final revision.
Representation: build entries from the rule a i j equals f of i j; the number of possible orders is the divisor count of N; and the number of matrices over a k-set is k to the m n.
The three operations: addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise; multiplication is the row-times-column sum over the shared index.
The cautions that ride with multiplication: it is not commutative, the identity leaves a matrix unchanged, and a zero product does not force a zero factor.
The transpose laws: transpose of a transpose is A, it distributes over sums, scalars ride through, and — the crucial one — a product's transpose reverses the order.
Symmetric means A transpose equals A, skew means A transpose equals minus A, and every square matrix is the unique sum of half A plus A transpose and half A minus A transpose.
The entry counts: n times n plus one over two for symmetric, and n times n minus one over two for skew.
The special types — idempotent, involutory, nilpotent, orthogonal — and the trace identity that the trace of A B equals the trace of B A.
The inverse: defined by A times A inverse equals I, the product rule reverses the order, transpose and inverse commute, and the row-reduction method takes A beside I to I beside A inverse.
And one deliberate pointer forward: the determinant test for invertibility and the adjoint formula arrive in the next chapter, Determinants.
Finally, the rapid-recall card — the one-glance summary to run through the night before the exam.
